title: Reaction to a vaccine: what is normal
what: After a vaccine the body builds protection, and sometimes you can feel it. Most reactions are mild and pass on their own in 1 to 3 days.
why: For everyone after a vaccine, for yourself and for your child.
duration: normal reactions usually pass in 1 to 3 days
tell_doctor: What reactions you had to past vaccines
If your child has had seizures with fever

prepare.title: Fever medicine
prepare.text: Keep at home the fever reducer your doctor advises for your age or your child's.

prepare.title: Phone
prepare.text: Write down the phone number of the clinic where the vaccine was given.

steps: Stay at the clinic for the first 30 minutes after the shot
At home, watch how you or your child feel and the injection spot
Redness and a firm lump up to a few centimeters across are usually normal
A mild fever, weakness or fussiness in the first 1 to 2 days is also normal
With a fever, offer more drinks and light clothing
Give a fever reducer if the doctor advised it
After some live vaccines, a reaction can come later, after 5 to 14 days. Ask your doctor
feel: Most often the injection spot aches
There can be weakness and poor appetite
after: Do not rub or warm the injection spot
Tell the doctor about a strong reaction before the next vaccine
red_flags: Trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, a rash all over: call your local emergency number
Seizures or loss of consciousness: call your local emergency number
Very high fever that does not come down, or a child crying nonstop for several hours: see a doctor urgently
The injection spot is very swollen, hot, with pus: see a doctor

faq.q: If there is no reaction, did the vaccine not work?
faq.a: No. Protection builds even without a noticeable reaction.

faq.q: Can we go out after a vaccine?
faq.a: Usually yes, if you feel well. Avoid getting chilled and crowds on the first day.

reminders.text: Vaccine given? Watch how you feel for 1 to 3 days. Keep a thermometer and fever reducer handy.
